title: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate · Units 03–04
description: Curated dictionary skills, dictionary entry conventions, language-study terminology, parts of speech, word formation and pronunciation.
sourceNotice: Prepared from user-supplied reference pages. Vocabulary targets follow the source topics; example sentences and teaching notes are newly written. Source exercises, extended passages, and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching sections, figures, exercises and relevant answer-key entries checked for vocabulary and construction coverage.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA for short targets and source-indexed entries; connected speech and accent variants are not exhaustively represented. Optional IPA may be blank if a reliable transcription was not established.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Teaching-page and illustrated exercise comparison; answer-key and pronunciation-index consultation; editorial and linguistic checks; static JSON schema and TTS target validation.
audit.limitations: Live VocabLab browser import and text-to-speech playback have not been performed; audio behaviour depends on the runtime.

units.title: Unit 03 — Using a dictionary
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 12–13 (PDF pages 13–14).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Choose suitable bilingual and English-language dictionaries for different needs.
Read dictionary entries, part-of-speech labels, pronunciation symbols, usage examples, and countability marks.
Use common defining language and distinguish several meanings of the same word.
Check spellings, silent letters, verb-preposition combinations, and frequent collocations.
Use context and example sentences to select an appropriate meaning or translation.

items.example: A bilingual dictionary helped me translate the phrase.
items.note: A dictionary that gives information in two languages.

items.pt: dicionário de inglês; dicionário monolíngue de inglês
items.example: An English dictionary provides definitions and examples in English.
items.note: A dictionary written in English rather than translating every entry.

items.example: I check unfamiliar words in an online dictionary.
items.note: Many learner dictionaries are available on the internet.

items.example: You can look up a word before using it in an email.
items.note: Look up means find information in a dictionary or reference source; also look it up.

items.example: Check the pronunciation before practising the new word.
items.note: The way a word is spoken; note the spelling differs from pronounce.

items.example: The dictionary uses a phonemic symbol for each speech sound.
items.note: A symbol representing a phoneme, usually shown between slashes.

items.example: The dictionary tells you the part of speech of each entry.
items.note: A word category such as noun, adjective or verb.

items.example: Read the definition and then check the example.
items.note: A statement explaining what a word means.

items.example: The dictionary labels fun as an uncountable noun.
items.note: In dictionary entries, [U] means the noun is uncountable.

items.example: For fun is a fixed phrase you can learn as a unit.
items.note: A conventional group of words whose wording is usually stable.

items.pt: palavra que costuma aparecer com outra; colocação
items.example: Good is a common word partner of idea.
items.note: A word that is frequently used with another word.

items.example: Important phrases appear in bold in this entry.
items.note: Describes text printed with thicker, darker letters.

items.example: The example sentences are shown in italics.
items.note: Describes sloping type used to distinguish some text.

items.example: We sometimes practise English songs just for fun.
items.note: Means for enjoyment rather than for a practical reason.

items.example: Have fun at the party tonight!
items.note: An informal expression wishing or describing enjoyment.

items.pt: zombar de alguém; tirar sarro de alguém
items.example: It is unkind to make fun of someone’s accent.
items.note: To laugh at or joke about a person in an unkind way.

items.example: Can you define this term without translating it?
items.note: To explain what something means.

items.example: The lecturer emphasised the need for regular revision.
items.note: Give special attention or importance to something. British spelling; US: emphasize.

items.example: The article contains words relating to the environment.
items.note: Introduces a connection or relationship between things.

items.example: The exercise is connected with the previous lesson.
items.note: Common pattern: connected with or connected to something.

items.example: The amount of information in this entry is useful.
items.note: Used especially with uncountable quantities; number is common with countable things.

items.example: You need an official document to confirm your identity.
items.note: Approved or produced by a person or organisation in authority.

items.example: Children do not always behave the same way at home and at school.
items.note: Act in a particular way; related noun: behaviour.

items.word: put a tick next to something
items.pt: colocar uma marca de verificação ao lado de algo
items.example: Put a tick next to each expression you have checked.
items.note: In British English a tick (✓) indicates a check or approval.

items.pt: deduzir o significado; tentar adivinhar o sentido
items.example: Try to guess the meaning before opening your dictionary.
items.note: Use context to work out what an unfamiliar word means.

items.example: Check a translation in an English dictionary before using it.
items.note: Different translations can fit different situations.

items.example: Read through all the meanings to find the right one.
items.note: Read something from beginning to end, often carefully.

items.example: This word has a different meaning in that sentence.
items.note: A word may have more than one sense or use.

items.example: I always check the spelling of difficult words.
items.note: One l after a; not allways.

items.example: That definition is really helpful.
items.note: Usually written with double l; not realy.

items.example: Unfortunately, the website is unavailable today.
items.note: Contains fortunate plus -ly and the negative prefix un-.

items.example: I enjoy short stories, especially mysteries.
items.note: Spell with es- at the start, not ex-.

items.example: I packed warm clothes for the journey.
items.note: Plural noun; distinguish clothes from cloth.

items.example: These chairs are comfortable for studying.
items.note: Often pronounced with three syllables in British English.

items.example: We booked accommodation near the station.
items.note: British English: usually uncountable; spell with double c and double m.

items.example: They walked through a beautiful garden.
items.note: Spelling: beauti- + -ful; not beautifull.

items.example: The final score was almost unbelievable.
items.note: Spelled un-believ-able: use -ie- after l, not -ei-.

items.example: A dictionary is useful but not always necessary.
items.note: Spell with one c and double s.

items.example: The letter k is a silent letter in knee.
items.note: A written letter that is not pronounced.

items.example: The island is a short boat journey from the coast.
items.note: The letter s is silent.

items.example: She hurt her knee while playing tennis.
items.note: The initial k is silent.

items.example: Keep a small comb in your bag.
items.note: The final b is silent.

items.example: The town has a castle near the river.
items.note: The t is silent.

items.example: We had salmon and vegetables for dinner.
items.note: The l is silent.

items.example: Could I have a receipt for this purchase?
items.note: The p is silent.

items.example: The town has a large industrial area.
items.note: Adjective: relating to industry.

items.example: They donated a large sum to the charity.
items.note: Here sum is a countable noun meaning an amount of money.

items.example: The children pretended to be astronauts.
items.note: Often followed by to + infinitive or a that-clause.

items.example: She received a certificate after the course.
items.note: An official document giving evidence of a fact or achievement.

items.pt: nem um pouco; de forma alguma
items.example: I am not at all worried about the result.
items.note: Adds emphasis to a negative statement; also has a separate polite-response use.

items.example: The company requested legal advice.
items.note: Adjective: relating to the law.

items.example: Their new puppy sleeps beside the sofa.
items.note: A young dog.

items.example: We need to organise the notes by topic.
items.note: British English also accepts organize; American English usually uses organize.

items.example: This pronunciation exercise is extremely useful.
items.note: An adverb of degree, often modifying adjectives or other adverbs.

items.example: Could you give me some advice about my studies?
items.note: Uncountable noun: some advice or a piece of advice, not an advice.

items.example: You can rely on this dictionary for clear examples.
items.note: Verb + preposition: rely on someone or something.

items.example: An old friend called me after many years.
items.note: Can mean someone you have known for a long time, not necessarily an elderly person.

items.example: My best friend lives in another city.
items.note: A very close friend, often the person you feel closest to.

items.example: She quickly made friends with her new classmates.
items.note: Use make friends with; not do friends with.

items.example: A close friend helped him prepare for the interview.
items.note: Close describes a strong personal relationship.

items.example: Please send the form by post before Friday.
items.note: British English, the system for sending mail; US English usually mail.

items.example: Has any post arrived for me today?
items.note: British English, the letters or parcels you send or receive; usually uncountable.

items.example: She applied for a teaching post at the college.
items.note: A formal countable noun for a position or job.

items.example: They attached the notice to a wooden post.
items.note: A countable noun for an upright piece of wood or metal.

sectionsChecked: A: What dictionaries do I need?

units.title: Unit 04 — English language words
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 14–15 (PDF pages 15–16).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Name and recognise major English parts of speech and articles.
Distinguish countable and uncountable nouns and regular and irregular verbs.
Recognise phrasal verbs, common phrases, prefixes, suffixes, and derived forms.
Understand phonemic symbols, syllables, word stress, and basic pronunciation terminology.
Use common punctuation terms and apply word-building patterns.

items.example: Nouns and verbs are two different parts of speech.
items.note: Categories used to describe how words function in a sentence.

items.example: Window is a noun in this sentence.
items.note: A word for a person, thing, place, idea, or quality.

items.example: She is a pronoun that can replace a person’s name.
items.note: A word used in place of a noun or noun phrase.

items.example: Listen is a verb in the expression listen to music.
items.note: A word expressing an action, event, or state.

items.example: Brown is an adjective in brown chair.
items.note: A word describing a noun or pronoun.

items.example: Quickly is an adverb describing how she walked.
items.note: A word modifying a verb, adjective, another adverb, or a clause.

items.example: By is a preposition in by the window.
items.note: A word connecting another element to a noun phrase, often indicating place or time.

items.example: The is the definite article in the English language.
items.note: The points to something understood as specific or identifiable.

items.example: An is an indefinite article in an elephant.
items.note: The forms a and an introduce a nonspecific singular countable noun.

items.example: And is a conjunction joining two ideas.
items.note: A word that links clauses or other language units.

items.example: So is a link word that can introduce a result.
items.note: A word used to connect ideas and show their relationship.

items.example: Book is a countable noun, so we can say three books.
items.note: A noun that has singular and plural forms and can be counted.

items.example: Information is an uncountable noun.
items.note: Normally not used with a/an or a regular plural in its uncountable sense.

items.example: We found useful information on the course website.
items.note: Uncountable in standard English; do not use informations.

items.example: Work is a regular verb because its past form is worked.
items.note: Forms its past tense and past participle in the usual -ed way.

items.example: Take is an irregular verb: take, took, taken.
items.note: Does not form all past forms simply by adding -ed.

items.example: Wake up is a common phrasal verb.
items.note: A verb combined with a particle, and sometimes an additional preposition.

items.example: Please take your shoes off at the door.
items.note: Separable phrasal verb in the clothing sense: take them off.

items.example: I wake up early on weekdays.
items.note: Intransitive in this example; past tense: woke up.

items.example: I am working from home at the moment.
items.note: A fixed time phrase meaning now.

items.pt: não se preocupe; deixa pra lá
items.example: Never mind, we can try again tomorrow.
items.note: Said when a problem or mistake does not matter.

items.example: See you later after the class.
items.note: An informal expression used when leaving.

items.example: Word building helps you recognise related forms.
items.note: Creating words by adding prefixes or suffixes or combining elements.

items.example: Un- is a prefix in unhappy.
items.note: A group of letters added at the beginning of a word.

items.example: The word kindness contains the suffix -ness.
items.note: A group of letters added at the end of a word.

items.example: The old chair was uncomfortable after an hour.
items.note: Formed from comfortable with negative un-.

items.example: The answer is incorrect, but the method is useful.
items.note: The prefix in- gives correct its opposite meaning.

items.example: I dislike studying in a noisy room.
items.note: The prefix dis- reverses the meaning of like.

items.example: There has been a clear improvement in her writing.
items.note: A noun formed from improve with -ment.

items.example: The brochure has an attractive design.
items.note: An adjective formed from attract with -ive.

items.example: A phonemic symbol shows a particular speech sound.
items.note: Dictionary transcriptions often place phonemic symbols between slashes.

items.example: Cinema has three syllables in British English.
items.note: A spoken unit centred around a vowel sound.

items.example: The stress in before falls on the second syllable.
items.note: Prominence given to one syllable; not the psychological meaning of stress.

items.example: The stressed syllable in cinema is the first one.
items.note: The syllable pronounced more prominently in a word.

items.example: Please finish the form before Monday.
items.note: Two syllables; stress on the second: be-FORE.

items.example: They opened a new cinema in the town centre.
items.note: Three syllables; stress on the first: CIN-e-ma.

items.example: Check your punctuation before sending the message.
items.note: Marks used in writing to separate sentences and clarify meaning.

items.example: Begin each sentence with a capital letter.
items.note: A large letter used at the start of sentences and in names.

items.example: Put a full stop at the end of a statement.
items.note: British English; American English usually period.

items.example: Use a comma after the opening phrase.
items.note: A punctuation mark that can separate clauses or list items.

items.example: Take a short pause before the next sentence.
items.note: A brief stop in speaking or an activity.

items.example: A direct question usually ends with a question mark.
items.note: The punctuation sign used at the end of a direct question.

items.example: That hotel is too expensive for our budget.
items.note: An adjective that can come before a noun such as hotel.

items.example: I never leave a dictionary entry without checking an example.
items.note: An adverb of frequency, normally placed before a main verb.

items.example: The message uses informal language.
items.note: Three syllables; stress on the second.

items.example: Find the opposite of the adjective in the list.
items.note: Three syllables; stress on the first.

items.example: We need to decide which translation fits.
items.note: Two syllables; stress on the second.

items.example: Education can provide more career opportunities.
items.note: Four syllables; the main stress falls on -ca-.

items.example: These notebooks are cheap but good quality.
items.note: Adjective; adverb: cheaply.

items.example: We bought the tickets cheaply during a promotion.
items.note: Adverb formed by adding -ly to cheap.

items.example: Driving in thick fog can be dangerous.
items.note: Adjective; related adverb: dangerously.

items.example: The driver was travelling dangerously fast.
items.note: Adverb formed from dangerous with -ly.

items.example: It was kind of her to explain the mistake.
items.note: Describes someone considerate; not the noun meaning type.

items.example: It would be unkind to laugh at his mistakes.
items.note: Opposite of kind, formed with un-.

items.example: She showed great kindness to the visitors.
items.note: Noun formed from kind with -ness.

items.example: We were lucky to catch the last train.
items.note: Adjective; opposite: unlucky.

items.example: He was unlucky to miss the final question.
items.note: Adjective formed from lucky with the negative prefix un-.
